commentary.bottom_line: Three offline replay studies found that re-testing after a software update, over time, or in a new trial setting detected performance losses that recalibration or brief adaptation then recovered. No study tested local reassessment in a live deployment, measured patient outcomes, or evaluated the equity reassessment the recommendation calls for.

perspectives.view: All three tests of the practice are level 4 retrospective replays in offline settings. They agree in direction, with performance falling after change and recovering after local adjustment. Certainty is very low because the designs are observational and simulated, and no study measured whether revalidation changed clinical decisions or patient harm.

An updated software version used at the old threshold had specificity of 23.1% versus 45.8% and produced 36.4% more diagnostic testing, and it matched its predecessor only after recalibration. In a separate benchmark, naive quantization dropped AUROC to 0.500, which a plausibility filter raised to 0.699. These results suggest that routine updates can silently break validated performance.

In a real deployment in India, sensitivity rose from 68.4% to 99.6% and specificity fell from 96% to 64.7% between validation and implementation. Expanding a fax model to new clinics coincided with lower performance. One adaptation study needed 20 events per end point to transfer a trial-derived tool, which suggests local retesting may be feasible with modest labeled data.

No test of the practice reported subgroup or equity metrics. Hazard studies show that performance shifted in a rural safety-net setting in India, and that three language models followed explicit non-US guidelines 30.0-36.7% of the time versus 76.7-86.7% for US guidelines. These findings may indicate that populations far from the development setting carry more risk.

In a Canadian simulation of 319,012 patients, AUROC fell from 0.807 to between 0.670 and 0.677 by 2022-23, and updating on the full data restored it. This suggests revalidation is a recurring cost rather than a single event. The adaptation study suggests the labeling effort per new context may be small, though no study reported staff time or cost.

When an updated tool ran at an unrevalidated threshold, specificity fell by about half and diagnostic testing rose by 36.4%. For patients, this may mean more follow-up tests, more false alarms, and more worry. Recalibration before release brought performance back to the prior level in that study.

commentary.research_gap: The evidence lacks a prospective study in live care that compares deployments with and without pre-release local revalidation and measures clinical decisions, patient harm, and subgroup performance. No study tested revalidation of large language model updates, fine-tuning, or retrieval changes, and none reported the staff time and cost of repeated validation.
commentary.underserved_note: The three tests of the practice included older adults in Viet Nam and a racial and ethnic minority focus in Canada, but none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The safety-net and non-English contexts appear only in hazard studies, so health systems serving these groups have evidence that performance can shift for their patients but no evidence on how well local revalidation corrects it.
